author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Quebec Conservative Marc Damant says Nunavik needs a local MNA
content:
Nunatsiaq News reached out to each candidate running in the Ungava riding ahead of Quebec’s Oct. 5 provincial election. Here’s what Quebec Conservative party candidate Marc Damant had to share with us.




Marc Damant says he wants to represent Ungava because Nunavik needs a local representative in the Quebec national assembly.




“I think it’s time that Nunavik had someone who was more of a full-time MNA,” said Damant, who lives in Kuujjuaq and is the Quebec Conservative party’s candidate in the Oct. 5 provincial election.




He said that previous MNAs didn’t enough of an interest in the region, and that people feel like they don’t matter.




While he acknowledged logistical and financial challenges make it difficult for candidates to visit Nunavik’s villages, he said nothing beats face-to-face conversation with electors.




“We have to do better for everyone,” said Damant, adding he’s the only candidate with posters up in Kuujjuaq right now.




Damant works as an airport manager for the Kativik Regional Government, where he’s responsible for airport operations and safety for multiple communities across Nunavik. From 2007 to 2014, he was a grounds operations co-ordinator for Air Inuit, a role that allowed him to travel across Nunavik.
















He also spent 11 years as a reservist in the Canadian Armed Forces and previously taught in China, Akulivik and La Tabatier

title: Iqaluit’s low-barrier shelter to open in January
content:
Uquutaq Society’s new $40-million low-barrier shelter is slated to open in Iqaluit in January.




The new building is located downtown at 158 Nipisa St., near The Snack Restaurant.




Uquutaq Society’s emerging new three-storey facility includes 44 low-barrier shelter beds on the second floor and 13 single-room transitional housing units on the top floor. The main floor will be a warming centre during the day. (Photo by Daron Letts)




“This is a low-barrier site, meaning you don’t need to be sober or unimpaired [to enter],” said society CEO Laurel McCorriston in an interview in September.




Named by elders as Ullivik, which means “the place you wait for the tide,” the three-storey, 44-bed facility will offer

 16 beds for women, 24 beds for men and two rooms for 

couples, which can also serve as private space for individuals in need of quiet or privacy.




The building includes an additional 13 single-occupancy transitional housing units on the top floor.




Currently, the only other low-barrier facility in the city is the society’s 17-cot overnight shelter at 534 Niaqunngusiariaq Road, which accommodates five women and 12 men nightly.

title: Tusaajiapik elders home residents being relocated to Montreal
content:
Residents of Kuujjuaq’s Tusaajiapik elders home are being relocated to private facilities in a Montreal suburb 1,500 kilometres south.

The relocation is part of a three-way agreement that also includes Argyle Inc.’s long-term housing and care centre, a private seniors home in the Montreal suburb of Pointe-Claire.




“The agreement aims to provide for a safe, caring and culturally sensitive living environment, including 

occasional access to traditional food and the support of three Inuit workers,” Wednesday’s statement continued.




Once all residents have been relocated, Tusaajiapik will close.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Nunavik beneficiaries to see a 25% gas subsidy increase
content:
The Kativik Regional Government and Makivvik increased the gasoline subsidy for Inuit beneficiaries nearly 25 per cent Thursday.




The subsidy went to $1 per litre from 78 cents, following an a 32-cent jump in gasoline prices, according to a joint press release issued Wednesday.




“Gasoline in Nunavik is not a luxury. It is what allows people to get out on the land, harvest food, visit family and move within their communities,” Makivvik president Pita Aatami said in the release.




The subsidy is available for James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement beneficiaries.




Before the price and subsidy increases, beneficiaries were paying $1.69 per litre of gas. Now they will pay $1.78.




This subsidy is part of a wider suite of “cost-of-living” subsidies, to which the provincial government recently promised $155 million over the next six years, according to the release.




The other five subsidies impact food, airfare, harvesting equipment, elder assistance and household appliances.

title: Amélie Béchard hopes to maintain CAQ hold on Ungava
content:

Amélie Béchard isn’t a career politician. She says she decided to run for office in Ungava with the Coalition avenir Québec because she wants to make a difference.




“I’m here for the people,” said Béchard, speaking to Nunatsiaq News from her hometown of Matagami.




The candidate hopes to replace former Coalition avenir Québec member Denis Lamothe, who held the seat for two terms, from 2018 to 2026.




“I could be a strong voice in Quebec City — bringing our issues to the forefront, defending them, and helping our region grow,” said Béchard, who visited Whapmagoostui and Kuujjuarapik last week.

She has also sat on boards of directors, such as the economic development society of Baie-James and Matagami’s business development society.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: I’m growing older than my anaanatsiaq will ever be
content:
Not everyone has the privilege of growing up with their grandparents presence and knowledge. It’s a blessing I didn’t have.




My anaanatsiaq was Tookasie Akpaleeapik. When my family, who is from Pond Inlet, was chosen to help the Inujjuarmiut (families from Inukjuak) adjust during the High Arctic Relocation in the 1950s, she followed to Grise Fiord.




Author Larry Audlaluk mentions my grandmother in his memoir 

What I Remember, What I Know: The Life of a High Arctic Exile

.




“When we arrived in Grise, after the aircraft’s engines stopped and the pilot opened the door to let us out, none of us wanted to be the first to get out. We were too shy. Tookashie was the brave one, getting out first.”




After the relocation she was sent to Churchill, Man., where she attended residential school. After graduation, Tookasie Akpaleeapik moved to Ottawa to practise nursing.




She took her own life shortly after, and that loss still affects my family. Grief doesn’t just magically go away over time; it stays with us throughout generations.




Everyone remembers her as a strong young woman who wasn’t scared to follow her dreams, regardless of hardships.
















Her soul is still shining bright through my oldest sister, Maggie Tookasie, who was given my anaanatsiaq’s name by my anaana (mother) Katie Koonoo.

author: Daron Letts
title: Orange Shirt Day moves indoors in rainy Iqaluit
content:
Hundreds of Iqalummiut gathered inside the cadet hall for the sixth annual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. It was a testament to the resolve of Indigenous Peoples who Canada’s residential school system tried to separate from their culture, language and traditions.




“We are still here,” said Gloria Uluqsi, the president of Nunavut Tunngavik Inc., the territory’s Inuit rights-holding organization.




Uluqsi seemed to hold back tears as she spoke from the podium, alternating between Inuktitut and English.




“We have endured so much,” she said. “Our families experienced hurt and loss. Inuit were separated from their families, their language, their culture and their way of life.”




Also known as Orange Shirt Day, the event remembers the experience of the estimated 150,000 Inuit, First Nations, and Métis children who attended 139 residential schools across Canada from the 1880s until as late as the 1990s.




“There’s elders, there’s youngsters — everybody from all walks of life,” said Eva Michael, communication specialist for event host Qikiqtani Inuit Association, as she observed more than 250 people pour into the building shortly after noon.

content:
For the English version of this story, please see

.

ᑭᓕᒃᕙᒃ ᑲᑉᓘᓇ ᐃᓚᐅᓂᐊᓯᔪᖅ ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ




“ᐱᒃᑯᓇᑦᑎᐊᕐᑐᖅ,” ᑲᑉᓘᓇ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 17-ᒥ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




ᓯᕗᓂᐊᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᓚᐅᖅᑎᓐᓇᒍ ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᑐᙵᕕᒃᑯᓐᓂ, ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᓐᓄ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᒥᓂᔅᑕᓄ ᑐᒡᓕᕆᔭᐅᔪᓄᑦ, ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐃᓅᓯᖃᑦᑎᐊᕐᓂᕐᒥᓐ, ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᔪᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐃᒻᒥᓃᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᓂ.




ᑕᐃᑲᓂᓕ ᐃᑲᔪᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᒃᓴᖅᑖᕋᓱᖕᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᐊᖅᑯᓴᕆᐊᖅ ᒪᒥᓴᕐᕕᒃᒧᑦ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂᑦ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ, ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖅ ᒪᓕᒃᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᔪᓂᒃ ᓱᓕᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑲᒥᓴᓐᑯ ᐊᑐᖁᓯᒪᔭᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐱᐅᓯᕚᓪᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᑦ ᒪᒥᓴᖅᐸᓪᓕᐅᔾᔪᑎᒃᓴᖏᓐᓂ.




“ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᖃᕐᓂᓐᓂ ᑕᑯᓯᒪᕗᖓ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓐᓇᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᖃᓄᐃᙱᓐᓂᕐᓴᐅᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᓅᖃᑎᒌᑦᑎᐊᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᒪᐅᓇ ᐊᑐᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᒃᑯ  ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᔪᓂ,” ᑲᑉᓘᓇ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.
















ᐋᓐᓂᐊᖃᖅᑕᐃᓕᓂᕐᒥ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᕐᓂᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᐅᓯᕚᓪᓕᒃᑲᓐᓂᕆᐊᖃᕐᒪᓐ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. ᐅᓄᕐᓂᕐᓴᐃᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᑖᒃᑯᓇᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᕐᓴᐅᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᒪᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᖅᓴᕐᕕᒃᓴᓂ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᖃᕐᓗᓂ, ᑖᓐᓇᑦᑕᐅᖅ ᓇᓗᓇᐃᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᖓᓂ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




“ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᒃᓴᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᑲᐅᑎᒋᔪᓐᓇᔾᔮᙱᑦᑐᑦ, ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᒃᑰᖓᓂᖓᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᐃᓐᓇᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒥᒃ, ᐅᓇ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᑐᐃᓐᓇᐅᙱᑦᑐᖅ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᔫᓴᕝ ᒨᑖᒃ-ᕙᓚᐅᕙᔅ, ᐃᓚᐅᓕᕐᓂ ᐱᒋᐊᓕᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔩᑦ ᒫᔅᓯ 2025-ᒥ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑲᑉᓘᓇᒎ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᑦᑎᐊᕐᓇᕐᒪᓐ ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᕐᓂᑰᓪᓗᓂ ᐅᖃᐅᔾᔪᐃᔨᐅᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᓕᒪᓂᕐᓴᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᒻᒥᓃᖅᑎᑦᑎᑦᑕᐃᓕᓂᕐᒥᒃ.




“ᐱᓇᓱᑦᑎᐊᒻᒪᕆᖕᒪᓐ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᑦᑎᐊᖅᖢᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᔭᕆᐊᓕᖕᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᕐᒧᑦ. ᐊᒃᑐᐃᓯᒪᓂᖃᕐᒪᓐ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᑯᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᑕᒪᑐᒧᖓ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᒨᑖᒃ-ᕙᓚᐅᕙᔅ.




ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᑲᑎᒪᔩᑦ ᐱᑕᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᑲᓇᑕ ᒪᓕᒃᑲᓗᐊᕐᒪᖔᑦ

Sonia Caron said she never saw herself going into politics. Her decision to run for MNA in the Ungava riding came after four parties approached her.

A lifelong supporter of the party from Chibougamau, Caron has spent the last 25 years working in education. She serves as the director of professional development at the Centre de services scolaire de la Baie-James, which oversees trades programs in northern Quebec.




She said her priorities are the lack of frontline health services and clean drinking water in many remote communities, issues that need to be treated with urgency.

The 

$75-million, 64,500-square-foot facility started production at 60 per cent capacity Sept. 23, said operations director Jason Gibbons in an interview.

author: Daron Letts
title: Joy and remembrance on National Day for Truth and Reconciliation schedule
content:
Joy and celebration are on the schedule for many of the events throughout Inuit Nunangat for the sixth annual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday.




“Truth and Reconciliation Day is a day where we take a good look at ourselves and we realize that we’ve made it,” said Tylie Arnatsiaq, head co-ordinator with Igloolik’s Artcirq performance troupe. 

“It’s a good reason to have a joyful event as a community.”







Also known as Orange Shirt Day, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation was established in response to Call to Action 80 of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.




It called on the federal government to collaborate with Indigenous peoples to create a holiday to recognize survivors, their families, and communities while ensuring the history and legacy of residential schools are publicly remembered.




Artcirq has acrobatic acts, a clown show and a juggling routine scheduled to follow a walk and a feast at Igloolik’s community hall on Wednesday afternoon.




“We will feed the community,” said recreation coordinator Qumangaapik Arnatsiaq.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Jason Iqaluq wins Hudson Bay byelection
content:
Jason Iqaluq will be the new MLA for the Hudson Bay constituency in Nunavut’s legislative assembly after winning Monday’s byelection over Nukaja Sala.




Iqaluq received 168 of the 228 ballots cast, while Sala received 54, according to Elections Nunavut’s website. Voter t

urnout was 48.61 per cent, with 228 of the 469 eligible voters casting ballots.




Voting took place Sept. 28 at the council chamber in Sanikiluaq. Advance voting was available from Sept. 14 to 24 at the hamlet office, and a mobile poll was held Sept. 21.




Iqaluq has lived in Sanikiluaq, the sole community in the Hudson Bay riding, his entire life. He works as a station team leader at the community’s airport and has served on the board of the local Arctic Co-op for about nine years.




The Hudson Bay seat became vacant after former MLA Daniel Qavvik resigned June 1. He was elected in 2022.

title: Ungava needs progressive option, Québec solidaire’s Antoine Côté says
content:
Nunatsiaq News reached out to each candidate running in the Ungava riding ahead of Quebec’s Oct. 5 provincial election. Here’s what Québec solidaire candidate Antoine Côté had to share with us.




Québec solidaire’s Antoine Côté says he’s the most progressive option for Ungava voters in Quebec’s Oct. 5 provincial election.




While the young climate activist based in Montreal is not from any community in Ungava — the province’s largest riding by area — he said voters, especially Inuit and Cree, need to be able to vote for a party that’s doing more than others to listen to them.




“We’re the only party in Quebec with an internal commission dedicated to representing First Nations and Inuit peoples,” he said. “They have real political power inside of our structure and they advise the party on Indigenous affairs, and one of their biggest contributions to our platform is cultural safety and fighting systemic racism.”




He mentioned that Quebec’s last election, in 2022, Québec solidaire candidate Maïtée Labrecque-Saganash finished second, receiving 24.5 per cent of Ungava’s vote. The party, he says, is a popular option.

title: Iqaluit photographer’s Nunavut Quest picture featured in Toronto exhibit
content:
Dustin Patar is excited for himself and for other photojournalists across Canada who currently have their work displayed at Toronto’s Union Station.




Patar, an Iqaluit resident, was in Toronto on Monday for the media preview of Points of Departure, an exhibit that showcases pictures from 16 photographers.




“These photos are from across Canada and Canada is a big country,” he said, adding many citizens are uninformed about various parts of the country. “I think these photos, including mine, are a way for them to kind of experience a little bit of that.”




Patar’s picture focuses on two women, 

Jennifer Quassa

 and 

Lindsay Kalluk

, who were travelling across the Arctic in April to report on the

title: New airport terminal opens in Rankin Inlet
content:
Community members and politicians gathered at the Rankin Inlet airport Monday morning to celebrate the opening of its new terminal.




The event featured a qulliq lighting, prayer, ribbon-cutting and a barbecue, wrote Department of Transportation and Infrastructure spokesperson Greg Belanger in a public service announcement.




“The new larger air terminal building is a key transportation hub for the community of Rankin Inlet and the Kivalliq region, connecting people, goods and communities across Nunavut and the rest of Canada,” he wrote.




Transportation Minister George Hickes, Rankin Inlet South MLA Annie Tattuinee, Nunavut MP Lori Idlout, and Northern and Arctic Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand attended the ceremony.




Nunatsiaq News requested an interview with Hickes, but he was unavailable.




Chartrand was set to make a funding announcement on behalf of federal Transportation Minister Steven MacKinnon, according to the release.




Belanger did not respond to questions about the announcement.

author: Daron Letts
title: Iqaluit bylaw investigation ongoing 1 month after dog attack
content:
A dog attack that led to an 11-year-old girl being medevaced to Ottawa for surgery is still under investigation by the City of Iqaluit more than a month after the incident.




“The city does not have an update or findings to share at this time, and I can’t provide a date for when they will be available,” city spokesperson Geoff Byrne said in an email on Sept. 24, one month after Mia Joy Nowdlak-Fraser was mauled by a dog tethered in a backyard near a downtown playground.




Bylaw officers were not available to explain their investigation methodology, Byrne added.




On Aug. 28, the owner surrendered the dog to the municipality. On Sept. 3, it was killed.




On Aug. 25, an RCMP officer approached Nowdlak and her daughter, but the family felt uncomfortable and declined to speak, Nowdlak said in an interview Friday. No bylaw officer or city official has ever approached the family, she said.




She said her daughter is doing “OK” and she continues to support her.

ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖓ ᔮᓐ-ᕗᕌᓐᔪᐊ (ᔨᐊᕝ) ᐴᓂᐄ ᑐᓴᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᐊᕕᒃᑐᖅᓯᒪᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᓄᑦ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 15-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᕋᓛᑦ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᓂᑯᓂ ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᐅᑎᖏᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᖅᑕᐅᔪᒪᓂᖏᑦᑎᒍᑦ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᐅᒃᐱᕈᓱᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᒃᑲᓐᓂᕋᓱᒡᓗᑎᒃ ᑭᒃᑯᓕᒫᓂ ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᓐᓂ.




ᐅᑯᐊ ᐱᒋᐊᖅᑐᕕᓃᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᔪᕕᓂᕐᓄᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᔪᓚᐃ 2025-ᒥ ᐸᓖᓯᓕᕆᓂᕐᒥ ᓄᓇᕕᒃᒥ ᑖᒃᑯᐊ ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᑦ ᐱᖓᓱᐃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᑐᖂᑎᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋ ᑕᒫᓂ ᑕᖅᑭᑦ 8 ᐃᓗᐊᓂ. ᑎᓴᒪᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ – 6-ᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓕ ᐊᕐᓇᖅ – ᐃᓅᔪᓐᓃᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐸᓖᓯᒃᑯᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑕᐅᓂᖏᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᖅᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᓕᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ.




ᒪᐃᒥ ᑕᑯᔭᐅᔪᓐᓇᕐᓯᑎᑕᐅᓂᑰᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐅᓇ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᓯᓂᖅ ᐃᓚᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ 35-ᓂ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᓯᒪᔪᓂᒃ. 21 ᑖᒃᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᕋᓛᓄᑦ, 8 ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᖅᑕᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᒪᓕᒋᐊᖃᕐᓂᖃᖅᑐᓂᒃ, ᑕᓪᓕᒪᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᖅᑕᐅᙱᖢᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᑕᐅᓯᖅ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐅᕈᑎᒋᔭᐅᙱᖢᓂ.

content:
There was a lot of talk about listening in Rankin Inlet this week.




Naalagit — or Listen, in English — was the theme of the Kivalliq Trade Show.




It was impressive to see how closely the speakers embraced that simple theme in their speeches.




Political and business leaders such as Sen. Karetak-Lindell told delegates Wednesday that listening to communities, youth and businesses can give us all a better understanding of their goals and aspirations. Communication must go both ways — speaking and listening — to make conversations productive and to lead to action, she said.

title: My travels as a small-town Inuk woman
content:
Annie Qimirpik




For someone from Kimmirut, a community of roughly 450 people, travelling out of town means getting on a plane, just like everywhere else in Nunavut.




There are no roads connecting us to the rest of the territory, let alone the rest of Canada. If you want to go somewhere else, you leave by air.




I grew up surrounded by vast landscape and in a very small population where everybody knows everybody. Often, everybody knows everybody’s business. There’s comfort in that kind of familiarity but there are also limitations. The world can feel far away.




This summer, over the course of six weeks, I travelled from six places: Iqaluit, Ottawa, Toronto, London, U.K., Clyde River and Cancun, Mexico.




Each was different and they gave me another way of looking at home.

Advance polls for the Ungava riding in Quebec’s provincial election open Saturday, and staff from the provincial elections authority will be in each Nunavik community to help make voting more accessible.




Élections Québec spokesperson Julie St-Arnaud-Drolet said visiting remote communities ahead of the Oct. 5 election day is part of an effort to address the historically low voter turn out in Nunavik. “Last election, electors in Inuit communities didn’t receive their reminder cards, for example,” St-Arnaud-Drolet said about the 2022 election, in which they weren’t able to reach some residents because they didn’t have access to their post office box addresses.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Iqaluit resident starts fundraiser to support John Amagoalik’s care in Nunavut
content:
An online fundraiser is collecting money for the medical needs of John Amagoalik, revered by many as the “Father of Nunavut.”




Amagoalik, 78, had been residing at the Embassy West long-term care home in Ottawa after a surgery forced the partial amputation of one of his legs. He was lonely there, he has said, and eager to return to the territory he helped create through decades of land claim negotiations.




He returned

running out

Iqaluit resident Jessica Hale, who describes herself on GoFundMe as a qallunaaq that cares deeply about social justice, created the fundraiser and set a $50,000 target. If reached, the amount could cover about three months of his care.




“John Amagoalik dedicated more than 25 years of his life to creating Nunavut,” Hale wrote on her GoFundMe page.




The fundraiser, which had raised $2,600 as of Thursday morning, was created on Sept. 18.




Amagoalik has 

filed a civil suit

 against the department, seeking a judicial review of the Health Department’s decision not to fund his care.

content:

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Coast Guard officer wins ITK award for Inuit excellence
content:
Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami is celebrating an Inuk leader with the Canadian Coast Guard by giving them its Award for Inuit Excellence.




ITK President Natan Obed presented the award to Ciera Avinga Lee-Kooneeliusie during the national Inuit organization’s annual general meeting Sept. 10 in Kuujjuaq.




She will receive a $2,500 cash prize as well as tickets to attend ITK’s annual Tapiriit gala next year in Ottawa.




Lee-Kooneeliusie serves as a senior search and rescue program officer with the Coast Guard. She also holds a position as one of the Arctic Region’s lead first aid instructors, ensuring first aid training includes Inuit knowledge.




Raised in Pangnirtung, Lee-Kooneeliusie is the first Inuk woman to hold a leadership position within the Coast Guard’s Inshore Rescue Boat Program in Nunavut, said a Sept. 10 news release from ITK about the award.




She is known for supporting opportunities for Inuit within the Canadian Coast Guards programming that highlight recruitment, mentorship and training, the release said.




The ITK Awards have been presented annually for more than 20 years. This year’s Award for Inuit Excellence received 41 nominations.
















Last year’s recipient was Diana Neill-Anawak, for providing culturally responsive speech-language therapy.

author: David Venn
title: Nunavut community organization receives $5.5M grant
content:
A non-profit in Nunavut has received a $5.5-million grant from the philanthropic arm of a mining company.




The money will go toward Annauma Community Foundation’s consensus granting program, which funds community-led initiatives across the territory, said a joint news release from Annauma spokesperson Lisa Milosavljevic and BHP Foundation spokesperson Nayomi Alexander.




BHP Foundation is a non-profit funded by BHP, an international mining company that specializes in iron ore, copper and metallurgical coal.




To date, Annauma’s program has awarded $4.3 million.




“This investment will benefit not only Annauma, but also Nunavut’s non-profit and charitable sector for years to come,” said Annauma co-founder Udlu Hanson in the release.




The grant will also support the Pirujaq Fund, which contributes to Annauma’s “long-term sustainability,” according to the release.




The Annauma Community Foundation focuses on “support for greater self-determination for Indigenous Peoples and preparing underrepresented young people for the future through education,” the release said.

title: Iqaluit council rejects renaming sewage lagoon ‘Trump Lake’
content:
A call to rename Iqaluit’s sewage lagoon Trump Lake died without a vote after no one seconded deputy Mayor Kim Smith’s motion during Tuesday night’s council meeting.




“I figure if (U.S. President Donald Trump) can rename landmarks, then so can we — and we can share a very polite Canadian giggle while we do,” Smith said as she presented her motion, adding no sign would be erected nor any public funds used if the lagoon were to be “symbolically renamed.”




Trump has signed executive orders to rename two bodies of water — the Gulf of Mexico in February 2025 and Lake Ontario in August. The new names, Gulf of America and Lake America respectively, are officially changed in the U.S. government’s Geographic Names Information System, and all federal departments and agencies must follow suit. 

But the change does not apply outside the United States.




In her roughly three-minute pitch, Smith expressed her opposition to several of Trump’s actions, including his threats to take over Greenland, the Iran war, and the ongoing trade war with Canada.




The U.S. president has repeatedly mused, joked and threatened to make Canada the “51st state,” and his aggressive use of tariffs has caused economic uncertainty across the nation.

title: NTI president extols the power of an ‘informed Inuk’ at Kivalliq Trade Show
content:
The world is changing fast, as are interests in the North. There’s pressure to mine Nunavut’s natural resources and to develop infrastructure projects that support Arctic security and sovereignty.




That’s why Inuit need to listen to each other, to their communities and to their youth, says Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. president Gloria Uluqsi.




Big decisions lie ahead about the impacts of future economic activity.




“An informed Inuk is much harder to leave out of a decision that affects them,” Uluqsi said Tuesday in a speech to the Kivalliq Trade Show in Rankin Inlet this week.




She didn’t mention any projects by name. But there has been talk at the trade show about Agnico Eagle Mines’ gold mining and exploration, as well as the four nation-building projects going through the federal government’s Major Projects Office.




Those projects are the Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Project, the Grays Bay Road and Port Project, a hydroelectricity generator near Iqaluit, and a deepsea port in Qikiqtarjuaq.




Uluqsi leaned into the trade show’s theme — Naalagit, or “Listen” in English. She spoke about what it means to listen and what it means to be heard.

title: From ‘Fore!’ to ‘Play ball!’: Golf event makes Iqaluit minor softball league reality
content:
Minor league softball is coming to Iqaluit in summer 2027, thanks to more than $220,000 raised by the Iqaluit Charity Golf Tournament in Gatineau, Que.




“This support will give more young people a chance to be active, learn new skills and take part in organized recreation,” said Iqaluit Mayor Solomon Awa Monday in a news release.




Organized by Outcrop Communications, more than 130 golfers took part in the Sept. 17 event, which also attracted approximately 30 corporate sponsors.




The donations are destined for the Ikajuqtiit Community Association, a non profit, Iqaluit-based organization that enhances recreational opportunities for local youth, including improvements to the Iqaluit ball diamond.




The funds will cover uniforms and equipment for the new league, said association chair Tom Fitzgerald Tuesday in a phone interview. 

The money will also pay for the installation of artificial turf in the outfield.




Those materials are scheduled to arrive next July on the first sealift of 2026, at no charge by Nunavut Sealink and Supply Inc., he said.




It is the first time the association has been the beneficiary in the charitable event’s 19-year history.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: GN ready to airlift fuel to Igloolik if needed after shipment delayed 9 days
content:
The Government of Nunavut is on hand to fly diesel up to Igloolik, but officials don’t expect it will be needed.




The hamlet’s annual resupply of fuel was initially expected to arrive Sept. 17. That shipment has been 

delayed

 by nine days and now is expected to arrive Saturday.




Igloolik relies on diesel fuel for generating electricity, home heating and for the trucks that provide drinking water and sewage services. With reserves dwindling, the hamlet had asked residents to conserve water, and put the water trucks on a reduced schedule.




John Ivey, Igloolik’s senior administrative officer, said the hamlet has since lifted these restrictions after the territory assured him that the community wouldn’t be left without fuel.




The territory’s Petroleum Products Division is prepared to airlift fuel to the community if necessary, said Greg Belanger, a spokesperson for Transportation and Infrastructure Nunavut.




“The [petroleum products division] is closely monitoring inventory, and while we do not currently anticipate the need to airlift fuel, the option is available if required,” Belanger said.




The hamlet had approximately 80,000 litres of diesel fuel in its tanks as of Sept. 18, he said, an amount that should be “sufficient until resupply.”
















The department did not explain why the Igloolik’s fuel shipment was delayed.

content:
An Inuit cultural organization in Nunavik is criticizing Quebec’s decision to conduct its Oct. 5 provincial election entirely in French.

The move abides with Quebec’s language law, which

His organization says Inuit voters will be disenfranchised if they have to navigate the provincial election in a language they don’t understand.




According to data collected in Nunavk in 2021, 8,770 out of 13,985 Indigenous respondents, or 62 per cent, reported they speak English only. A total of 1,550 respondents, or 11 per cent, reported they don’t speak English or French.

author: Daron Letts
title: Former Iqaluit mayor launches AI-driven site to monitor municipal issues
content:
How many new homes can Iqaluit’s water reservoir support?




Former Iqaluit mayor Kenny Bell is using artificial intelligence program ChatGPT to investigate this question and more, on his newly launched City Hall Record website.




The idea, Bell said, is to track long-term municipal issues that may have fallen by the wayside.




“I’m engaging as a citizen that’s also interested in our community,” Bell said Friday in a phone interview. “It’s really hard to go on the city website and find minutes and listen to records and stuff — especially if you don’t know what you’re looking for.”




Bell was elected to a four-year term as Iqaluit mayor in 2019. He

mandatory water conservation efforts

Turns out, people in Iqaluit love to take a polar dip for a good cause.




About 90 people gathered at Apex beach Sept. 17 to jump into icy Frobisher Bay to raise awareness for suicide prevention.

ᑮᓇᐅᔭᒃᑯᕕᒃ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐊᑐᖅᑐᐊᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 9−ᒥ ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᐊᖑᔪᒥ.




ᓯᕗᓪᓕᖅᐸᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᐅᔪᒥ ᑕᑯᓂᐊᖅᐳᖅ 4.2-ᒥᐊᒐᐅᐊᑦ ᐊᓄᕆᒨᖅᑐᒥ ᐸᐅᕋᐅᑎᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ 4-ᒥᐊᒐᐅᐊᑦ ᐆᒻᒪᖅᑯᑎᒧᑦ ᑐᖅᑯᖅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᓯᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᓕᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᓴᓂᓕᐊᓂ ᐅᔭᕋᖕᓂᐊᕐᕕᖓᓄᑦ, ᐃᓂᖃᖅᑐᒥ 125 ᑭᓛᒥᑐᐸᓗᖕᓂ ᓂᒋᖅᐸᓯᐊᓂ ᐃᖃᓗᒃᑑᑦᑎᐊᕐᒥ.




ᓂᕆᐅᒋᔭᐅᕗᖅ ᑐᓂᓯᓂᐊᕐᓂᖓᓂ 20 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᑲᑉᐱᕼᐃᓕᖅᑑᑉ ᐆᒻᒪᖅᑯᑎᖏᓐᓂ ᐱᔭᕆᐊᓕᖏᓐᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐊᓄᕌᕐᔪᐊᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒥᒃᖠᒋᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᓗᓂ ᐅᔭᕋᖕᓂᐊᕐᕕᐅᑉ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᑕᒫᒥ ᐅᖅᓱᐊᓗᑐᐃᓐᓇᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ 7 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒧᑦ, ᐅᖃᐅᓯᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐊᒡᓂᑯ ᐄᒍᓪᑯᓐᓂ.




“ᑕᑉᐹᓂ ᐊᓄᕆᖃᕐᔪᐊᖅᑐᐊᓗᒃ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐊᒡᓂᑯ ᐄᒍᓪ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᑉ-ᑐᖏᓕᖓ ᑯᕆᒡᑕᕗ ᐋᑕᒻᔅ ᐅᖃᓘᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᐱᖅᓱᖅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᑎᑎᕋᕐᕕᖓᓂᑦ ᑐᕌᓐᑎᒥ. “ᐅᓇ ᖁᕕᐊᔾᔪᑎᒋᕐᔪᐊᖅᐸᕗᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᕐᓂᕐᒥᕐ ᐊᑕᐅᓯᕐᒥ ᐸᐅᕋᐅᑎᒥᒃ. ᐸᕐᓇᒃᐳᒍᑦ ᓴᓇᓂᕐᒥ ᑎᓴᒪᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓂ.”

title: Nunavut RCMP encouraged to continue wearing name tags
content:
While on-duty RCMP officers are no longer required to wear name tags on their uniforms nationally, Nunavut RCMP are going in a different direction.




Officers are encouraged to continue wearing name tags, with their names in English and Inuktitut syllabics as well, said an unsigned statement provided to Nunatsiaq News from the Nunavut RCMP.




The email lists three Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit principles as the Nunavut RCMP’s foundation: Inuuqatigiittiarniq, which means respecting others; tunnganarniq, or fostering a welcoming spirit; and aajiiqatigiingniq, which is reaching consensus through discussion.




The RCMP made the country-wide change to make name tags option on March 30, according to reports from the Globe and Mail.




Britt Bancroft, board director with the National Police Federation, the union that represents members and reservists with the RCMP, said the change was in response to officers being doxxed and having their families identified and harassed.




“We’re supportive of the option to remove name tags and instead display their badge for accountability when members feel a situation is unsafe,” Bancroft said in a statement to Nunatsiaq News.

title: Five candidates run for Ungava riding in Quebec election
content:
Five candidates are running in Quebec’s largest riding by land mass, which includes Nunavik, in the Oct. 5 provincial election.




Ungava MNA Denis Lamothe, who has held that seat since 2018, announced in January he would not seek re-election. His Coalition Avenir Québec party has nominated Amélie Béchard instead.




Originally from Matagami, she is a forestry engineer who specializes in operations management and forest planning. She has served on several boards of directors including the Matagami Commercial Development Corp.




The Parti Québécois nominated Sonia Caron, who manages the Baie-James Vocational Training Centre in Chibougamau.




In a statement posted on the party’s website, Caron said she hopes to give more decision-making power to northern communities, protect Indigenous Peoples’ ways of life, and ensure communities benefit from the North’s resources.




“I will be proud to be the first woman elected Member of the National Assembly for Ungava, and the first Indigenous person to represent this voice,” she said.




Antoine Côté will represent Québec Solidaire.
















Côté ran for councillor in Montreal in the 2025 municipal election. Parti Solitaire’s website does not yet list a biography or campaign priorities for Côté but says the information will be added.

author: Randi Beers
title: A case for rent control in Nunavut
content:
As temperatures drop and we start to prepare for another fall, we’re reminded of one of Nunavut’s most urgent problems: housing.




Andrew Morrison




We don’t need another study to make us aware of the crisis. We see it every day not only on the streets of Iqaluit, but in other, more hidden ways: students coming home with nowhere to live, families crammed into relatives’ homes and long-time Iqalummiut losing their staff housing when they retire. Too many people face various forms of homelessness in their own homeland.




The numbers back this up. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. reports that Iqaluit’s rental vacancy rate was just 0.3 per cent in 2025 — six empty units out of nearly 2,000. That leaves tenants with almost no alternatives and lets rents climb far beyond what many can afford.




Nunavut should freeze rents.




Rent control won’t solve the whole housing crisis. It won’t build the homes we badly need, and it won’t house everyone who is currently without shelter. But a rent freeze will help address staggering rental rates that seem to be going up every time we blink. 




Rent control won’t lower today’s already high rates, but it would limit how fast they can rise in future. Right now, Nunavut’s Residential Tenancies Act allows landlords to raise rent once every 12 months, with three months’ written notice — but sets no limit on the size of the increase.

title: Igloolik close to running out of fuel
content:
Igloolik is close to running out of fuel after an annual delivery didn’t arrive on time.




John Ivey, the hamlet’s senior administrative officer, said the Government of Nunavut told him the shipment that was expected to arrive Sept. 17 will now come on Sept. 26.




“It’s delayed for some reason,” he said in an interview.




Igloolik relies on diesel fuel for generating electricity to heat homes and for the trucks that provide drinking water and sewage services.




He said the hamlet is encouraging residents to conserve water and to limit electricity use.




“We got some assurance from the GN that they won’t let the town run out of fuel,” he said. “If it gets to the point where it’s getting pretty close, there could possibly be an airlift of fuel brought in, but we’re not at that stage.”




The hamlet has also contacted Nunavut’s emergency measures organization and local rangers, he said, who are prepared to help out if the shipment doesn’t arrive in time.
















He said technicians with the GN’s petroleum products division are in the community monitoring the situation and providing guidance. 




 “We’re pretty confident that they’re doing a good job keeping an eye on things,” Ivey said.

title: ‘Listen up,’ say Kivalliq Trade Show organizers
content:
The Kivalliq Trade Show hasn’t started yet and it’s already breaking records.




With 60 exhibitors and more than 240 delegates, next week’s event is the biggest to date, says Kivalliq Trade Show Society president Robert Connelly.




“And our delegate numbers will keep going up as the event nears,” he said in a phone interview on Thursday.




With ongoing discussions about Arctic sovereignty, resource extraction and developing northern infrastructure, 

organizers are emphasizing the need to bring Inuit to the table, Connelly said.




“There has to be a lot of listening to make sure that the people of Nunavut and particularly Inuit are strongly engaged,” he said.




That idea is reflected in this year’s theme: Naalagit, the Inuktitut word for “listen.”




The panel discussions were built with that theme in mind. The first is called “Listening to Communities,” the second “Listening to Business” and the third “Listening to Youth.”
















Panelists across the three discussions include Christine Tootoo, vice-president of Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami’s National Inuit Youth Council; CBC journalist Juanita Taylor; historian Ryan Shackleton; and Albert Netser, with Arctic Fresh Projects.




Canada’s Arctic Ambassador Virginia Mearns is scheduled to give the keynote address on Tuesday morning, with other speakers such as Nunavut Senator Nancy Karetak-Lindell and Nunavut Tunng

author: Daron Letts
title: Arctic Talent: Dance like no one is listening
content:
John Manzo is Galaxy Cat, a multifarious artist who performs with panache.




He hosts the soundscape that animates the 200 guests who turn out to his twice-annual silent discos at Iqaluit’s Franco-Centre.




The fifth one is slated for Sept. 26. 




A silent disco involves three DJs spinning clashing genres of music that are pumped into participants’ headphones through radio frequencies. Each reveller tunes in to the channel of their choice.




Most come costumed. 




Fairies, astronauts, dinosaurs, fuzzy animals, pirates, space cowgirls, and at least one Cookie Monster have turned out to Galaxy Cat’s four past events.




Those without costumes don neon, fishnets, or just loud colours with unique hats or wigs.
















”Whatever makes you feel happy,” Manzo said.




The next event features DJ Miel who spins Latin music and house — a type of electronic music that speeds up to 130 beats per minute.




Beside her is DJ Will, whose musical taste is confined to the last two decades of the 20th century and the first decade of this one. 




Then there’s Galaxy Cat, who purrs for drum and bass — a 

sub-genre of electronic dance music with fast breakbeat drum patterns and heavy basslines.




“Because nobody else plays it in town,” Manzo said of why he chooses this style over others.




The opening hour belongs to Deadbeatz, who plays a mix of Afrobeats and disco.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Maggie Annahatak elected Kangirsuk mayor by 1 vote
content:
Maggie Annahatak has been elected mayor of Kangirsuk after edging out Noah Eetook by a single vote in Wednesday’s byelection.




Annahatak, who works as a housing manager with the Nunavik Housing Bureau, received 59 votes, while Eetook received 58. Lucy Tukkiapik Carrier received four votes, and two ballots were spoiled, according to results shared on the municipal services’ Facebook page Wednesday night.




Annahatak could not be reached for comment about her win on Thursday.




A total of 123 of Kangirsuk’s 337 eligible voters cast ballots, representing a turnout of about 36.5 per cent.




The byelection was held to fill the mayoral seat left vacant after Etua Kaukai died in July.




Kaukai was elected mayor on Nov. 6, 2024, for a three-year term. He also served on the board of Nunavik Investment Corp., a non-profit organization that provides funding and loans to entrepreneurs.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Kilikvak Kabloona joins National Council for Reconciliation
content:
A former CEO of Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. has been named to the group responsible for monitoring whether Canada is meeting its reconciliation commitments.




Kilikvak Kabloona is joining the National Council for Reconciliation.




“It’s a real honour,” Kabloona said in an interview Thursday.




Prior to working at the NTI, she was the Government of Nunavut’s associate deputy minister responsible for quality of life, a position focused on responding to the territory’s suicide crisis.




There, she helped secure funding for the Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre in Iqaluit, she said, a project that aligns with one of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s calls to action to improve Indigenous Peoples’ access to healing.




“Over my career, I’ve seen how progress can be made toward a healthier, more vibrant society through the implementation of these types of reports,” Kabloona said.




Health care in Nunavut still needs to get better, she said. More Inuit need to be working in that field and there needs to be more training available, which was also identified as a call to action, she said.
















“These things will take time, it is a process and it’s important that we continually work on reconciliation. It is not a check box exercise,” she said.

author: Daron Letts
title: Northern construction leaders call for more housing, local trades training
content:
Four big players in Nunavut’s construction industry achieved consensus within moments of the start of the “Builders Behind our Communities” panel Wednesday at the Nunavut Trade Show in Iqaluit. 




“Execution without capacity-building is not OK,” is how Arctic Fresh general manager Evan Schellenberg summed it up. He was one of four panelists who discussed how construction companies are involved in the communities where they build.




Schellenberg pointed out that even many of the delegates in the audience slept on couches the night before. 




“Every project must be seen as a housing project,” he said. “It can’t be a side note.”




The annual Nunavut Trade Show, which started Monday, gives business leaders a chance to meet and discuss ideas during four days of panel discussions, speeches and workshops.




While eyes across Canada are looking North with Ottawa spending billions to expand the country’s military presence in the Arctic, Nunavut’s housing crisis 

continues to worsen

. Twenty communities have a “critical” housing need, according the Nunavut Housing Corporation’s 2024-25 annual report.




Meanwhile, in Iqaluit, new housing is 

not keeping up

 with demand, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation said in its Northern Housing Report, released earlier this year. Iqaluit’s vacancy rate is 0.3 per cent, the report found.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Udlu Hanson named to top 100 most powerful women in Canada
content:
Baffinland Iron Mines Corp.’s vice-president of community and strategic development has been named to the Women’s Executive Network’s 104 most powerful women in Canada.




Udlu Hanson is the first Inuk from Nunavut to receive the honour since 2010, when Kathy Okpik, then the territorial deputy minister of education, was named. 




“That makes me grateful,” Hanson told Nunatsiaq News Wednesday from the Nunavut Trade Show in Iqaluit, where she took part in a panel discussion the day prior. 




“That makes me proud to represent the many, many strong Inuit women that have helped impact my career.”




The network released its 24th annual list last week, which celebrates CEOs, entrepreneurs, professionals and leaders in governance and artificial intelligence.




Hanson, who is also the president of the Baffin Regional Chamber of Commerce, has served as an executive at Baffinland for more than seven years. Before that she was a Government of Nunavut deputy minister and CEO of Nunavut Tunngavik Inc.




She said she’s inspired by women who give back to their communities like her mother Ann Hanson, a broadcast journalist and author who served as the third commissioner of Nunavut between 2005 and 2010.
















“There’s so many strong Inuit women who belong on that list,” Hanson said. “I think maybe we should have our own.”

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Nunavik police identify suspects in fires across 3 communities
content:
Nunavik police say they have identified suspects in a string of recent fires across Puvirnituq, Akulivik and Kuujjuaq.




Speaking Monday at the Kativik Regional Government council meeting in Inukjuak, Chief Jean-François Bernier said police arrested one person last weekend and that several suspects are children aged 12 and under.




The investigation covers incidents that occurred over several months. Investigators have ruled out that on serial adult arsonist could be behind the fires, said police public relations manager Julie Berthold in an email Wednesday.




Nunatsiaq News asked Berthold for a timeline and details of the fires that are being investigated but she declined to provide more information, citing the active investigation.




Many of the properties targeted are abandoned or unoccupied houses and shacks, Bernier told councillors during Monday’s meeting. He urged people in the affected communities to report sightings of anybody they see around these buildings at night.




“What I’m asking is that people call us immediately so that we send the patrol on the spot to catch them,” Bernier said.




Bernier said police have increased patrols in Puvirnituq, the most affected community, while investigators review what the chief described as hundreds of pieces of video evidence.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: John Amagoalik launches lawsuit, says he won’t return to Embassy West
content:
John Amagoalik has filed an application for judicial review at the Nunavut Court of Justice in response to the territorial government’s refusal to fund his medical care and housing. 




Steve Kelliher, his lawyer and longtime friend, said 

the Government of Nunavut has betrayed not only Amagoalik but also his dream of Inuit self-determination. 




“The colonial control from above is gone, and in its place is a form of a recolonization from below,” Kelliher said. “By that I mean the emergence of an executive class within Nunavut that the Inuit legislators give absolute deference to.”

 




Amagoalik’s family members paid for his care when he returned to Iqaluit earlier this June but needed more long-term support. The department 

informed

 them last month that wouldn’t be possible, since privately arranged care falls outside of its mandate.




“They do have legislative authority to do this, they just chose not to,” Kelliher said.




Kelliher argues the government’s actions contravene Section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, aimed at protecting citizens from being deprived of their rights to life, liberty and personal security. 




He is also requesting an urgent hearing through a separate application. He’s asking that Amagoalik immediately be provided with ongoing medical care and housing, which he says the family currently cannot afford.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Kangirsuk is holding election to fill mayor vacancy
content:
The community of Kangirsuk is holding a byelection to fill the mayoral seat, following the death of Etua Kaukai in July.




Lucy Tukkiapik Carrier, Maggie Annahatak and Noah Eetook entered the race, which is scheduled for Wednesday, from 12 p.m. to 8 p.m. Advanced polling took place Sunday.




Carrier has long served as the local representative for Kangirsuk on the Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services. She was elected chairperson of the board’s executive committee.




Annahatak currently works as a housing manager with the Nunavik Housing Bureau.




Nunatsiaq News attempted to get comment from each candidate. Annahatak declined. The other two did not respond.




Kaukai

 was elected mayor on Nov. 6, 2024, for a three-year term. He also served on the board of Nunavik Investment Corp., a non-profit that provides funding and loans to entrepreneurs.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Inuk filmmaker among recipients of Governor General’s Arts Award
content:
Filmmaker Zacharias Kunuk will receive a 2026 Governor General’s Award, the Canada Council for the Arts announced Wednesday.




Kunuk, who was appointed an Officer of the Order of Canada in 2002 and who received the Order of Nunavut in 2019, is receiving an Artistic Achievement Award, one of eight awards that recognize artists for their contributions to contemporary visual and media arts.




“I was honoured to be selected,” Kunuk said in an interview. “When I started my career, I never dreamed I would be doing this and receiving awards.”




The other recipients are Faye HeavyShield, a Kainai First Nations sculptor and installation artist based in Alberta and  Skawennati, a Kahnawakeronon multimedia artist based in Montréal, Québec, a Canada Council for the Arts news release said.




They will each receive $25,000 and a bronze medallion. They were selected by a peer committee of artists and arts professionals, the release said.




The award comes 25 years after the release of Kunuk’s first feature-length film, 

Atanarjuat: The Fast Runner,

 which he had hoped would coincide with the creation of Nunavut in 1999.




But the production ran into a year of funding difficulties, Kunuk said, as the filmmakers tried to secure support in a system dominated by English- and French-language productions.

author: Daron Letts
title: Public housing waitlist grew by one applicant per day in 2025, says Igluvut manager
content:
By the time the four-day Nunavut Trade Show wraps up in Iqaluit on Thursday, four more applicants will have been added to the territory’s housing wait list.




That’s because, last year, the housing waitlist grew by 365 applicants, says Aaron Pederson, project manager of housing and homelessness with Igluvut Corp., Nunavut Tunngavik Inc.’s housing non-profit.




“That’s one more family every single day,” he said.




That is one of several sobering statistics Pederson cited during Tuesday’s mid-morning panel discussion, “Building our territorial infrastructure”. The panel also featured Qikiqtaaluk Corp. President and CEO Harry Flaherty, Nukik Corp. senior project advisor Tom Garrett, and Kitikmeot Corp. President and CEO David Omilgoitok.




“In a territory with fewer than 10,000 occupied homes, the line for a house is more than 1/3 the length of the entire housing stock,” Pederson said.




Of the new homes being built, close to 95 per cent are public housing.




“Nationally, it’s six percent,” he said.
















Of the 61 per cent of Nunavummiut who live in public housing, 45 per cent live in overcrowded dwellings, he added.




Pederson suggested that those in charge of industrial projects “can’t staff positions from an overcrowded home.”




Igluvut, whose operations launched in April, provides an alternative housing model, he said.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Craig Simailak opens Nunavut Trade Show with call to seize opportunity
content:
Nunavut is looking for better co-operation with southern governments and businesses, as it prepares to bolster economic activity, says a territorial leader.




Community and Government Services Minister Craig Simailak made the comments Monday morning at the opening of the Nunavut Trade Show.




“Canada is paying great attention to the North,” he said at the Aqsarniit Hotel in Iqaluit. “How do we prepare for opportunities?”




In its 33rd year, the Nunavut Trade Show is hosting 106 exhibitors and 340 attendees. The event is running from Monday to Thursday and contains conference programming, a trade show and networking events.




The conference portion will take place at the hotel, while the trade show will take place at the Arctic Winter Games Arena.




The trade show is open to the public Thursday.




The four-day event will end on Thursday with a presentation for the Business Achievement Awards during the closing banquet at the hotel.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Lowering hiring standards for Inuit would create ‘2 classes’ of officers: Police chief
content:
Nunavik’s public security committee has rejected two recommendations aimed at increasing Inuit representation in the region’s police force, saying they would create unequal hiring standards.




Police Chief Jean-François (Jeff) Bernier gave an update to regional councillors Tuesday on the committee’s response to recommendations for reforming the police service and rebuilding public trust.




They stem from an audit 

launched in July 2025

 on policing in Nunavik after three fatal police shootings occurred in the region within eight months. A fourth person — a six-year-old girl — died during a police operation while the audit was being prepared.




Released in May, the audit 

includes

 35 recommendations. Twenty-one were supported by the committee, eight were conditionally supported, five were not supported and one received no comment.




One recommendation called for changes to the Quebec’s Police Act to give the regional government more authority to establish its own police hiring standards. Another called for Inuit applicants with certain criminal offences on their record to be exempt from automatic disqualification from employment in the police service.

author: David Venn
title: Nunatsiaq News wins several community journalism awards
content:
Nunatsiaq News received seven first-place finishes out of 12 honours overall at this year’s Canadian Community Newsmedia Awards.




Hosted by industry advocate News Media Canada, the annual competition included 654 entries in 29 categories for stories and photos published by English and French-language community newspapers across the country in 2025.




The results were announced Monday.




“This has been a heck of a year for Nunatsiaq News,” said managing editor Corey Larocque. “This year’s CCNA wins were all team awards, which says a lot about how our newsroom works.”




Nunatsiaq News won best all-round newspaper for its circulation size, which is between 1,500 and 6,499. 




The paper placed ahead of Town and Country This Week in Athabasca, Alta., and St. Marys Independent in St. Marys, Ont. Nunatsiaq News also won best editorial page and best front page.




“What a stellar newspaper,” said one judge’s comment. “Professional, clean looking, bilingual perfection.”
















Senior production artist Krista Klassen finished second for best ad design.




The rest of the categories the paper placed in were in a category with a circulation of less than 10,000, including Nunatsiaq News’s first-place finishes for best arts coverage and best community newspaper website.

author: Daron Letts
title: Inuit-owned companies seek private capital in Toronto
content:
Billions of dollars for infrastructure were on the menu at a Toronto luncheon hosted by the Government of Nunavut and Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. on Monday.




They organized the 90-minute event to coincide with the federal government’s inaugural Canada Investment Summit. The initiative 

brought together Inuit, territorial, private and federal investment leaders to huddle over the territory’s major infrastructure projects that need financial backers.




The two-day summit, hosted by Prime Minister Mark Carney, is billed as one step in a five-year plan to attract $1 trillion in investment over the next five years. 




“Our message is pretty clear right across all of these projects,” said West Kitikmeot Resources Corp. CEO Brendan Bell, in a phone interview on Monday. 

“We’re going to need private capital to step up if these projects are going to become a reality.”




The Inuit-owned company Bell represents is looking for funders for its proposed $1-billion Gray’s Bay Port and Road project, which features a proposed 230-kilometre all-season road and Arctic deepsea port.




In March, that project was referred to the federal government’s new Major Projects Office, a special operating agency supported by the Privy Council Office with the goal of advancing nation-building projects.




“If not now, never,” he said of the project’s funding timeline.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Two candidates to face off in Hudson Bay MLA by-election
content:
Jason Iqaluq and Nukaja Sala have put their name forward to replace former Hudson Bay MLA Daniel Qavvik ahead of a byelection scheduled for later this month.




Iqaluq has lived in Sanikiluaq — the sole community represented under the constituency — his whole life. He says he decided to run after others encouraged him. 




“There’s quite a few people that look up to me,” Iqaluq said.




Iqaluq works at the Sanikiluaq airport as a station team leader and has served on the board of his local Arctic Co-op for about nine years, contributing to the financial administration of the member-owned business. 




He said his priorities are housing, food security and improving access to health care, adding he’s 

happy to see that housing construction got underway this summer but that more units are needed.




“The community is growing,” Iqaluq said.




He said the care offered at the local health-care centre can be improved and that he’d also like to see a food bank open. 
















Meanwhile, Sala works as an administration assistant at the Qammaq Housing Association. She said through this role she sees first-hand how dire the housing crisis is.




“The conditions are getting worse every year,” she said about overcrowding and the community’s older, dilapidated homes.




Sala also said she wants to improve life for elders in the community by prioritizing them for new housing

content:

.

ᕿᑭᖅᑖᓗᒃ AEDC, ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᕿᑭᖅᑕᕐᔪᐊᖅᒥ ᐃᑎᔪᓂᒃ ᐃᒃᓴᕐᕕᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᕿᑎᕐᒥᐅᑦ ᐱᖓᓇᖓᓂ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑯᐊᐳᕇᓴᓐᑯᑦ, ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᒍᕇᔅ ᐸᐃ ᐊᖅᑯᑎᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑎᔪᒥᑦ ᑐᓚᒃᑕᕐᕕᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ, ᐅᖃᖃᑎᖃᑲᑕᒃᓯᒪᖕᒪᑕ ᓯᑯᑭ ᓅᒃ ᑲᖏᖅᖢᐊᓂ A/S ᐱᒋᐊᖅᖢᑎᒃ 2020-ᒥ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᕿᑎᕐᒥᐅᑦ ᐱᖓᖕᓇᖓᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᒥᑦ ᐳᕆᐊᓐᑕᓐ ᐱᐊᓪᒥ ᐊᐱᖅᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 1-ᒥ.




“ᑲᓛᖡᑦ ᓄᓇᖓ ᒪᓕᒍᒥᓇᕐᑐᖅ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕐᑕᖏᓐᓂ,” ᐱᐊᓪ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐅᖃᓘᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᑎᑎᕋᕐᕕᖓ ᑳᒍᕆᒥ. “ᐃᓱᒪᒋᓪᓗᒍ, ᐊᖏᓂᕐᓴᒃᑯᑦ, ᐱᖁᑎᒋᔭᐅᔪᑦ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᑐᓚᒃᑕᕐᕕᓕᕆᓂᖓᑦ.”




ᑲᒻᐸᓂᐅᔪᑦ ᐊᑎᓕᐅᓚᐅᕐᒪᑕ ᑐᑭᓯᖃᑦᑕᐅᑎᓯᒪᓂᕐᒥᒃ, ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᑎᑎᕋᕐᓯᒪᓪᓗᓂ ᑕᒪᐃᓐᓂ ᑐᕌᒐᕆᔪᒪᔭᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐅᒋᔭᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐆᒧᖓ “ᓴᙱᒃᑎᑉᐹᓪᓕᕋᓱᒃᖢᒋᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᑦ ᑕᕆᐅᕐᒥ ᐱᖁᑎᒋᔭᐅᔪᓄᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᓯᒪᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᑖᒃᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᖕᓂ, ᑎᑎᕋᖅᑕᐅᓂᑰᓪᓗᓂ ᐋᒐᓯ 31-ᒥ.




ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᓪᓚᕆᑲᑕᓕᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐊᖏᕈᑎᓕᐅᕈᒪᓂᕐᒥᒃ ᐊᕐᕌᒍ ᐊᑕᐅᓯᖅ ᐃᓚᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᑕᖅᑭᓂ 6-ᓂ.




“ᐅᑯᐊ ᑐᓚᒃᑕᕐᕖᑦ ᐃᖕᒥᖕᓄᑦ ᐅᖓᓯᒌᒃᑑᑎᐅᖕᒪᑕ,” ᐱᐊᓪ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ, “ᑭᓯᐊᓂᓕ ᐊᑕᐅᑦᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᒃᑐᐃᓂᕐᓴᐅᔪᓐᓇᕋᔭᕐᒪᑕ. ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᖁᕝᕙᖅᐹᓪᓕᕋᔭᕐᒪᑕ ᐊᒃᑐᐊᖃᑦᑕᐅᑎᒍᑎᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑕᐅᓰᕈᑎᐅᕙᒡᓗᑎᒃ ᐱᖁᑎᒋᔭᐅᓂᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐅᑭᐅᕐᑕᖅᑐᕐᒥ.”
















ᓲᕐᓗ ᐃᒪᓐᓇ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ, ᑐᐊᕕᕐᓇᖅᑐᖃᓕᕐᓂᖅᐸᑦ, ᒪᐅᓇ ᐃᒃᑲᑦᑐᒧᑦ ᐊᔪᓯᖅᑐᖃᕐᓂᕈᓂ ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ ᑯᕕᔪᖃᕐᓂᖅᐸᑦ ᑕᕆᐅᕐᒧᑦ, ᐅᒥᐊᕐᔪᐊᖅᑕᖄᓂᓕᖅᖢᓂ ᐅᑭᐅᕐᑕᖅᑐᕐᒦᑦᑐᓂᒃ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᕿᓚᒥᕈᓗᒃ ᐊᐅᓪᓚᖅᑎᑕᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᖢᑎᒃ.

author: Randi Beers
title: The Canadian roots of Donald Trump’s wealth
content:
Canadians are well aware that America’s boorish and vulgar president

 is wealthy. 




Donald Trump received a head start in life with money from his father, a real estate developer in New York who bent the rules and skirted legalities while amassing the wealth that he left to his children. 




Fred Trump set up trust accounts for his five children, of which Donald Trump was the fourth.

 By the age of three, he was earning the equivalent of US$200,000 per year in today’s dollars, or about C$276,000. At the time he graduated from college, he was receiving about US$1 million annually (C$1.38 million). 

By some estimates, he received over US$400 million (C$553 million) from his father.




Most of this is well known. Less well-known are the northern Canadian roots to the family’s fortune. 




In Kallstadt, Germany, in 1885, Donald Trump’s grandfather, Friederich Trump, was 16 years old and didn’t like the thought of working in the family vineyard or as a barber, a job for which he was being trained. So he left a note for his widowed mother and left home one night. He wanted to be rich and headed for Manhattan, eventually becoming an American citizen.

author: Randi Beers
title: News quiz Sept. 12 | Stranger than fiction
content:
It’s quiz time! Let’s roll.




1. An Ottawa-based non-profit is paying Nunavut teens to do what while scrolling their social media feeds?




A. Report the types of advertisements they are seeing.


B. Fact check viral social media posts.


C. Like and share posts about from the organization about media literacy.




2. Nunatsiaq News introduced readers to a new northern correspondent last week. What is different about her?




A. She is a licensed pilot.


B. She is a high school student.


C. She’s not human. She’s one of 121 AI “correspondents” that repackages existing news stories for a website based out of Hong Kong.




3. Oil spills are bad for the environment, but scientists are in Chesterfield Inlet studying one type of creature seems to benefit from it. What creature is that?




A. Sea cucumbers seem to love oil and grow to massive sizes when exposed to it.


B. There are naturally occurring microbes that feed off of oil.


C. Oil adheres to plankton floating in the water, making them shimmer, which makes them more visible to predators, like whales.
















4. A new development in Grise Fiord is making it easier for people to determine when it’s safe to travel. What is it?




A. Better radar and satellite imagery helps determine when precipitation is coming.


B. A new weather station about five kilometres east of the community shows real-time conditions.

title: ‘News’ site forces journalists to face future with AI
content:
The future arrived without warning two weeks ago, dragging Nunatsiaq News into the world of artificial intelligence controversy this paper had previously managed to avoid.




A journalist colleague at another organization sent an email, pointing out a new website that posts AI-generated articles about the North, based on news that real organizations had already reported.




We News appears to be a Hong Kong-based website using more than 100 AI-generated “correspondents” whose articles are cobbled together using artificial intelligence instead of traditional reporting. They gather their information from news articles written by real journalists and from official sources such as the RCMP and Government of Nunavut.




It calls its Nunavut correspondent Leah Qammaniq. She comes complete with an Inuit-sounding name, an AI-generated picture of a woman with Inuit features and even an AI-generated back story about being “raised in the North.”

news story

 about this troubling development. She did it the old-fashioned way by interviewing real people, researching the issue and sitting down in front of a computer to type it out.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Documentary on Inuit food, family set to screen in 3 Nunavut communities
content:
Nunavummiut have the chance to see a new documentary about Inuit food, resilience, culture and family this month as 

Nirilaurta: Let us Eat 

is set to screen in three communities.




The documentary follows the Ugyuk family of Taloyoak as they navigate high grocery prices and the cost of hunting equipment.




Malaya Qaunirq Chapman directed the film, which 

premièred

 Aug. 6 at the International First Peoples Festival in Montreal.




It’s scheduled to screen at 6 p.m. on Sept. 15, at Astro Theatre in Iqaluit, followed by a Q&A with Qaunirq Chapman, said Katja De Bock, a spokesperson for the National Film Board of Canada, in an email.




A screening in Rankin Inlet is set for Sept. 19 at 5 p.m. at the community centre. Another screening is scheduled in Baker Lake on Sept. 22 at 7 p.m. at the community hall.




All of the screenings are free.

He’s still alive after a cancer diagnosis and 10 rounds of chemotherapy.

went on to win Best Canadian Film at the Toronto International Film Festival, along with 25 other honours and is

content:

.







ᑕᒃᓯᓕᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐊᐅᓱᐃᑦᑐᕐᒥ ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᓚᐅᖅᑐᒥ, ᒫᑎ ᖁᓪᓗᒍᖅᑐᖅ ᖃᕋᓴᐅᔭᒃᑯᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᒋᐊᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐊᑦᑕᓇᙱᒃᑲᓗᐊᕐᒪᖔᑦ ᐊᐅᓪᓛᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ.




ᕗᕌᓐᓯᔅ ᒎᑦᑎᐊᐃ, ᐃᓕᓴᐃᔨᕐᔪᐊᖅ Université du Québec à Rimouski−ᒥ, ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᑦᑎᐊᒃᑲᓐᓂᖅᓯᕗᖅ ᑭᖑᓪᓕᖅᐹᖑᔪᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐃᓕᓯᓂᕐᒥ 10-ᒦᑕᓂ-ᖁᑦᑎᖕᓂᓕᖕᒥ ᓯᓚᓕᕆᕝᕕᖕᒥ ᐊᐅᓱᐃᑦᑑᑉ ᖃᓂᒋᔭᖓᓂ ᐋᒍᔅᑎ 15. ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒃ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓲᖑᕗᖅ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᖅᓯᕐᓂᕐᓂ, ᑕᕆᐅᑉ ᓯᑯᖓᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓯᒡᔭᖅᐸᓯᖓᓐᓂ ᓄᖑᑉᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᐅᔪᒥ. (ᑕᐃᕕᑦ ᑎᑎᐊᕐ ᐊᔾᔨᓕᐅᖅᑕᖓ)




ᐅᕘᓇ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥᓪᓗ ᓯᒡᔭᖅᐸᓯᖕᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕐᕕᐅᑉ ᐃᑭᐊᖅᑭᕕᖓᓐᓂ, ᖃᐅᔨᒋᐊᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᒫᓐᓇᓪᓚᕆᐅᔪᒥ ᐊᔾᔨᙳᐊᓂ ᓄᑖᖑᔪᒥ ᓯᓚᓕᕆᕝᕕᖕᒥ ᐃᓂᖃᖅᑐᒥ 5 ᑭᓛᒥᑐᐸᓗᖕᓂ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᒥᑦ.




ᑕᑯᒃᓴᐅᓂᖅ ᑕᑯᒃᓴᐅᑎᑦᑎᕗᖅ ᑕᖅᓯᖅ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓃᑐᐃᓐᓇᕐᓂᖓᓂ, ᖃᓄᐃᓐᓂᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᖓᓯᖕᓂᖅᓴᐅᔪᒥ ᓯᓚᑦᑎᐊᕙᐅᓪᓗᓂ.




“ᑕᐃᒫᒃ ᑲᔪᓯᓚᐅᖅᐳᒍᑦ ᓯᓚᑦᑎᐊᕙᐅᓂᐅᔪᒧᑦ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᖁᓪᓗᒍᖅᑐᖅ, ᕼᐋᒻᓚᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨᖓᑕ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᖓ.




“ᐃᑲᔪᕐᓂᖃᕐᔪᐊᖅᐳᖅ ᐱᓪᓚᕆᐅᔪᒥ, ᑕᑯᒃᓴᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᒫᓐᓇᓪᓚᕆᐅᔪᒥ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ.
















10-ᒦᑕᒥ-ᖁᑦᑎᖕᓂᓕᖕᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒃ, ᓴᓇᔭᐅᓚᐅᖅᑐᒥ ᑕᖅᑭᐅᓚᐅᖅᑐᒥ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᕗᖅ ᐊᖏᓂᖅᓴᐅᔪᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᐅᔪᒥ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᔪᒥ ᑎᐊᕆ ᓄᐊᒧᑦ, ᓇᖕᒥᓂᖃᖅᑎᐅᔪᖅ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᐊᐅᓪᓚᕈᔾᔨᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᐅᓪᓚᐅᔾᔨᔨ ᑲᒻᐸᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐊᐅᓱᐃᑦᑐᖅ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᓘᔭᕐᓂᕐᒥ.




ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖅ ᐱᓂᐊᖅᐳᖅ $300,000−ᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓄᑦ ᐱᖓᓱᓄᑦ ArcticNet−ᑯᓐᓂ, ᑲᓇᑕᒥ ᑮᓇᐅᔾᔭᒃᓴᕈᑕᐅᙱᑦᑐᒥ, ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᖅᓯᒧᑦ-ᐱᑎᑕᐅᔪᒥ ᓯᒡᔭᖅᐸᓯᖕᒥ ᓄᖑᑉᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑕᕆᐅᕐᒥ ᐊᓯᔾᔨᖅᐸᓪᓕᐊᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐊᐅᓱᐃᑦᑑᑉ ᐃᒪᕕᖓᓂ, ᓯᒡᔭᖅᐸᓯᖓᓐᓂ ᐅᖅᓱᖅᑑᒥ.




ArcticNet ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᔪᓚᐃ 29−ᒥ, ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᓪᓗᓂ $9.3 ᒥᓕᐊᓐᓂ ᑲᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐅᕗᙵᓚᐅᖅᑐᓂ 13−ᓄᑦ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᓯᒪᔪᓄᑦ- ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ-ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᔪᓂ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᐅᔪᓄᑦ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓄᓇᖓᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᖏᓂᖅᓴᐅᔪᒥ ᑲᓇᑕᐅᑉ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᖓᓂ.

title: Federal government ends NunatuKavut’s bid for Indigenous rights
content:
The federal government has ended a years-long process to negotiate Indigenous rights and self-determination with the NunatuKavut Community Council, an organization that says it represents about 6,000 Inuit in southern and central Labrador.




According to a Tuesday statement from NunatuKavut, Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty informed the council in a letter on Sept. 4 that the federal government was terminating its Recognition of Indigenous Rights and Self-Determination negotiations.




“[

NunatuKavut Community Council]

 is a strong and modern Inuit government that remains committed to the recognition of our rights and the advancement of our people’s well-being,” the statement read.




The council said it was not given substantive reasons for the decision.




The federal government has reviewed submissions from NunatuKavut, historical and legal analysis, expert reviews and discussions with the council, said Jennifer Cooper, a spokesperson for Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada, in an email to Nunatsiaq News.




The evidence provided by NunatuKavut did not meet “court-established tests for Indigenous rights and title,” Cooper said.




She said her department has offered to meet with NunatuKavut to discuss its findings in detail.
